title: Anti-Immigrant Furor in Thetford
author: Stephen F. Eisenman
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/thetford1.png)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/21/anti-
immigrant-furor-in-thetford/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/thetford1.png)

_Norwich Cathedral and close, August 12, 2026. Photo: The author._

**A long, hot, summer**

If William Blake were alive today, he’d call his country a “brown and
unpleasant land.” English summers used to be short and wet; now they are long
and dry. More than 70% of the country is experiencing drought, with hosepipe
bans and other water-use restrictions. Norwich, in the county of Norfolk,
where I live with my wife Harriet, has experienced its [hottest
summer](https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/cn8n9pg54m1o) ever, with a
record temperature of 36C (97F) on June 26, and multiple other days nearly as
hot. Yesterday (August 13) it reached 90. Today is expected to be the same.

Having lived in New York, Los Angeles, Chicago and Central Florida, the summer
warmth feels to me unexceptional, even welcome, what [Nat King
Cole](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7OZrNDtRltg) serenaded as “those lazy-
hazy-crazy days of summer.” But for people here, the excess of sun and heat is
punishing. In the age of global warming, Englishmen, contrary to Noel Coward’s
Depression-era patter song, avoid the [midday
sun](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n_el3Bo1ya8&t=7s). I suspect the same is
true of mad dogs.

Worse this summer than the heat, were the [race
riots](https://hopenothate.org.uk/2026/07/20/bicester-braintree-and-barnham-
neo-nazis-and-antisemites-infiltrate-local-protests/) and anti-immigrant furor
in London, Tamworth, Glasgow, Bicester, Wethersfield,
[Belfast](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/ng-interactive/2026/aug/08/how-
northern-ireland-race-riots-unfolded-belfast) and
[Thetford](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/aug/07/thetford-residents-
remain-on-edge-after-days-of-mob-rule-over-asylum-plans). They say hot weather
[increases aggression](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10303254/),
but anti-immigrant attacks have been a staple of British politics for
generations, and in all seasons. Notorious outrages include the Seaport Riots
of 1919, Notting Hill Riots in 1958, Northern Town Riots of 2001, and the
upwellings in Southport, Liverpool, Sunderland, Belfast, and Rotherham in
summer, 2024.

The most common argument British residents (especially white ones) make
against asylum seekers is that they cost the government money that could
otherwise be spent on services for them. But this is largely specious. The
[cost](https://obr.uk/forecasts-in-depth/brief-guides-and-explainers/public-
finances/) of the asylum system in the U.K. is 0.29 percent of the national
budget, and that could be reduced if asylum seekers were allowed to work in
jobs or industries where they are most needed. The other major complaint is
that newcomers – legal immigrants as well as asylum seekers -- undermine
traditional British values. I don’t mean to be ungenerous to my new hosts, but
apart from beer, chips, football and mistaken pride in a former empire,
British values are hard to identify. That’s not because values have broken
down, but because Britain has always been a diverse country. And anyway, the
taste for curries, kebabs, and pizza has long rivalled if not overtaken that
for pasties, baps, and bangers-and-mash.

The arguments against immigration and asylum are familiar and notorious. They
are found in Oswald Mosley perorations against London’s immigrant Jews in in
the 1930s; and again in 1958 and ’59 against Blacks from the Caribbean. A
decade after, Defense Secretary Enoch Powell rehearsed them in his [infamous
speech](https://anth1001.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/04/enoch-
powell_speech.pdf)given at a Conservative Party gathering in Birmingham.
Inveighing against a proposed anti-discrimination bill in parliament, he said
that the influx of Commonwealth immigrants was straining housing, hospitals,
and schools.

Most of all, however, Powell said immigration was polluting the nation, and
undermining both social cohesion and national values: “For reasons which
[British people] could not comprehend and …[about] which they were never
consulted, they found themselves made strangers in their own country.”
Claiming that immigrant communities aimed to organize themselves to replace
(“overawe and dominate”) native ones, he concluded: "As I look ahead, I am
filled with foreboding. Like the Roman [he’s referencing Virgil’s _Aeneid_], I
seem to see 'the River Tiber foaming with much blood.'"

Former Labor Prime Minister Keith Starmer, to his everlasting shame and
regret, echoed Powell’s “River of Blood” speech in an address from June 2025.
[He said](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj3rxrg2pnjo) that immigration
risked turning the nation into “an island of strangers.” Nigel Farage, leader
of the far right, Reform U.K. party, has gone farther, calling it an
“invasion” and “national security threat,” and promising if elected Prime
Minister, to greatly reduce immigration and ban all foreign nationals from
social housing and other public services, no matter how long they’ve been
legally settled.

In the U.K. as in the U.S., opposition to immigration and asylum has perverted
common sense. Even if you accepted the idea that mass immigration taxed
services, (not a point to be[
conceded](https://migrationobservatory.ox.ac.uk/resources/briefings/the-
fiscal-impact-of-immigration-in-the-uk/)), the current threat is non-existent.
The [number of U.K.
residents](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c70989jrdweo) who initially
came to the country seeking asylum is about 0.6 percent, in other words six in
a thousand. The number currently waiting for an asylum decision is 0.2
percent. The annual inflow of immigrants is 0.14 percent of the population,
that is, 1.4 out of a thousand. In addition, despite employment of seasonal
foreign workers in agriculture, there currently exist significant shortages of
workers in that and other sectors, especially healthcare, hospitality, and
construction. Economic growth in the U.K. depends upon the very labor pool
that most politicians are aiming to restrict. If the new PM, Andy Burnham,
wants to light a fire under the U.K. economy, he should start by denouncing
racism and embracing immigration. The Royal Navy could escort migrant boats
crossing the channel from France to England!

**The Thetford riots and Thomas Paine statue**

Norwich is only about 30 miles from Thetford (pop. 25,000), so on a hot Sunday
afternoon, four days after attacks there against immigrant and non-white
families, we decided to visit the town. The rock throwing, housebreaking,
window smashing and verbal abuse was over, the injured police had been treated
(one was badly bitten a rioter), the threatened residents were relocated, and
most of the press had gone. Thetford was buttoned up, and King’s Road, the
town’s high street, nearly deserted on the sunny, sabbath afternoon.

As we walked from the car park up the empty asphalt road, we passed on the
left a long, flint wall and on the right, some tidy, terraced homes of new
brick. Further on, a narrow road at left was lined with Georgian-era, grey
brick houses with shuttered shops below: a café, nail salon, and off license
(liquor and convenience store). In front of us, up King Street on the left,
appeared a golden apparition, a vertical invader standing on a two-step
plinth. It was Thomas Paine -- born in Thetford in 1737 -- all gilt and shiny,
like the swags and cartouches in Trump’s Oval Office.

His right hand grasped a quill pen, though from a distance it looked like he
was hailing a cab. His left held _Rights of Man_ (1791), a book written in
defense of the French Revolution. It’s upside down because Paine’s radicalism
turned politics upside down. Leaning right but looking left, his torso was
torqued, like a tornado. A revolutionary in three countries -- Britain, the
U.S. and France -- the association was apt.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/thetford2.png)

Sir Charles Thomas Wheeler, Thomas Paine, 1964, (outside King’s House,
Thetford,) August 9, 2026. On the plinth is written WORLD CITIZEN, ENGLISHMAN
BY BIRTH, FRENCH CITIZEN BY DECREE, AMERICAN BY ADOPTION. Photo: the author.

I wondered what the rioters in Thetford would have thought of Paine’s plan for
asylum seekers, contained in [_Rights of Man, Part
II_](https://thomaspaine.org/major-works/rights-of-man-part-the-second/):

> To receive all who shall come, without enquiring who or what they are. The
> only condition to be, that for so much, or so many hours’ work, each person
> shall receive so many meals of wholesome food, and a warm lodging, at least
> as good as a barrack. That a certain portion of what each person’s work is
> worth shall be reserved, and given to him or her, on their going away; and
> that each person shall stay as long or as short a time or come as often as
> he choose on these conditions.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/thetford3.png)

Thomas Paine, Rights of Man, parts 1 and 2, London: J. S. Jordan, 1791 and
1792. Collection: The author.

Paine added that the recent growth of manufactures in England, no less than
basic morality, demanded a plan for generalized
[asylum](https://thomaspaine.org/major-works/rights-of-man-authors-notes/):

> France and America bid all comers welcome and initiate them into all the
> rights of citizenship. Policy and interest, therefore, will, but perhaps too
> late, dictate in England, what reason and justice could not.

If the originalists on the current U.S. Supreme Court were true to their
principles, they wouldn’t have decided this year in favor of Trump’s policy of
turning back [asylum
seekers](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/press-release/supreme-
court-allows-trump-to-block-asylum-seekers/) at the border, nor revoked
temporary protected status for thousands of [foreign
nationals](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/how-the-supreme-court-became-
a-pivotal-force-in-trumps-immigration-agenda). In doing so, they rejected the
views of Paine, one of the nation’s founders.

I looked again at Paine’s statue and was impressed. Though modern
commemorative sculpture rarely escapes kitsch, this one was livelier and more
subtle than most. I wasn’t surprised to learn its author, Sir Charles Thomas
Wheeler, was for ten years (1956-66) president of the Royal Academy. His
sculpture recalls major works in the European cannon. From the _Moses_ of
Michelangelo (1512) and the _Statue of Liberty_ by Bartholdi (1886), Wheeler,
borrowed the idea of a figure carrying a massive law book – in Moses’ case,
the tablets of the Ten Commandments; in Lady Liberty’s case, a _tabula ansata_
representing the Roman legal system and the rule of law. Inscribed on the
latter is the date in Roman numerals, JULY IV MDCCLXXVI**"** (July 4, 1776),
the date of the Declaration of Independence, of which Paine is now believed to
have been an [author or editor](https://thomaspaine.org/the-sherman-copy/).
With its preamble, list of basic rights, and posting of grievances, the
Declaration reads like a bill of indictment founded in 18th C. English common
law. In his pamphlet _Common Sense_ (1776), Paine argued that in a just nation
“the law is king.” Fifteen years later, in _Rights of Man_ , he expanded the
idea, saying that people not governments are the ultimate lawgivers, and that
everyone is equal under law.

Wheeler was likely also familiar with Ernst Rietschel’s _Luther Monument_
(1861) in Worms, Germany, or the nearly [identical
work](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Martin-Luther-Denkmal_-
_Dresden,_Germany_-_DSC09227.JPG) by his student Adolf von Donndorf in
Dresden. There too, the figure stands on a stepped base and holds an oversized
book in his left hand. Luther’s bible symbolizes the Protestant idea of _sola
scriptura,_ meaning worship must be guided by the bible alone – holy law --
not the Pope, religious councils, or other authorities.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/thetford4.png)

Jean-Honoré Fragonard, Portrait of Louis-François Prault (formerly titled
Inspiration), 1769, Paris, Louvre; Sir Charles Thomas Wheeler, Monument to
Thomas Paine, 1964 (detail), Thetford, Norfolk, U.K. Photo: The author.

That Paine waged his revolution via the written word more than the rifle is
also suggested by the flamboyantly poised quill pen in his right hand. The
artist knew many paintings and sculptures of revolutionary figures carrying
swords or guns, for example the working man at left with saber and baldric in
Eugene Delacroix’s [Liberty Leading the
People](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix_-
_Le_28_Juillet._La_Libert%C3%A9_guidant_le_peuple.jpg) (1830); and Daniel
Chester French’s bronze statue of [The Minute Man
(1874)](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Daniel-Chester-French), based
upon a gunsmith and militia officer named Isaac Davis. But because Wheeler
wanted us to believe the pen is mightier than the sword, his Paine also
recalls the famous _Portrait of Louis-François Prault_ in the Louvre, one of a
series of “[Fantasy
Portraits](https://www.burlington.org.uk/archive/exhibition-review/fragonards-
fantasy-figures-washington)” by Jean-Honoré Fragonard. Paine’s exaggerated
features, tousled hair, and flamboyant ruff or _jabot_ , suggest a writer in
the throes of creativity. In both works, the subject’s pen is thrust left and
head turned right, echoing (in reverse) Cesare Ripa’s figure of “[Furor
Poetico](https://www.perspectivejournal.dk/en/girolamo-troppas-four-portraits-
of-ancient-philosophers/),” (“poetic inspiration”) from the  _Iconologia_
(1603).

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/thetford5.png)

Cesare Ripa, “Furor Poetico,” Iconologia, Rome 1603.

The figure’s gilding, a feature suggested by Wheeler’s patron, the [Thomas
Paine Historical Association](https://thomaspaine.org/about/our-history/) (of
the United States), also suggests energy and flamboyance. Napoleon is reputed
to have said to Paine in 1797, that he slept every night with a copy of his
_Rights of Man_ under his pillow, adding **“** a statue of gold ought to be
erected to him in every city in the universe.”

**Paine in Thetford in 1964…**

When the Paine monument was first proposed, it was criticized and even
condemned by some town residents. News of the controversy spread across the
pond. According to a report in [_The New York
Times_](https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1964/06/08/issue.html)(June
8, 1964):

> A member of the Thetford Town Council, John Mayles resigned in protest
> against unveiling a statue of a ‘revolutionary,’ a ‘traitor’ and an
> ‘anarchist.’ Mr. Mayles, an electrical engineer, calls himself ‘a truest
> blue, died in the wool Tory.’

The article’s tone was bemusement more than scandal. Paine was a New Yorker --
he died in Greenwich Village in 1809 -- and the Americans enjoyed
condescending to the British. But the stakes of the controversy in fact were
high. 1964 saw ‘Britain’s Racist Election,’ as it has [been
called](https://www.huffingtonpost.co.uk/2015/03/16/britains-racist-election-
channel-4-ukip_n_6876394.html), when the struggle over a single seat in
Smethwick near Birmingham galvanized the nation. There, the Tory candidate for
parliament, Peter Griffiths, rode a rising tide of racial resentment and took
the seat away from its long-time Labor MP. The unspeakable slogan in the
district was “If you want a n---r [my expurgation] for a neighbor, vote
Labor.” When challenged, Griffiths excused the sentence as a legitimate
“manifestation of poplar feeling.” Though the general election went to Labor,
the pattern of deploying racism to gain attention and political power, was
established. It would be used by Enoch Powell four years later, and nearly
every Tory since. It remains the bread and butter of Reform, and even Labor
has dined off it, as we have seen.

In Thetford in 1964, the placement of a gilded native son on a pedestal was
controversial because Paine was chief antagonist to Edmund Burke (veritable
founder of British conservatism), abolitionist, anti-monarchist, egalitarian,
atheist, and advocate for “the Commons,” as [Peter
Linebaugh](https://www.firstofthemonth.org/the-age-of-paine/) and [Jeffrey St.
Clair](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/07/05/the-global-revolution-of-
thomas-paine/)have written. The commons represented for him the ethic of
sharing and the satisfaction of actual needs, even if that mean ending -- by
force if necessary -- the swinish indulgences of the rich and powerful. True
sovereignty lies in the common people themselves, and that power must never be
alienated, even to elected representatives. He largely shared the view of his
friend and fellow revolutionary, [John
Oswald](https://archive.org/details/lettersfromfran00yorkgoog/page/n185/mode/2up),
that “as a man cannot piss by proxy, neither can he think by proxy.” That’s
why there was resistance among Conservatives in Thetford in 1964 to the
raising of a statue in honor of Thomas Paine. He [opposed
racism](https://thomaspaine.org/beacon/a-tale-of-two-toms-jefferson-and-
paines-radically-different-visions-of-america/), the most conventional yet
virulent of ideologies.

**…and now**

It’s thus a peculiar irony that one of the chief organizations in contemporary
Thetford that opposes the housing of immigrants is named the Thoman Paine
Independents (TPI). They recently changed their name to Thetford Sovereign
Council and then Thetford Council Watch. The new names recall the private
Citizen’s Councils and public Sovereignty Commissions that enforced
segregation in the U.S. South in the 1950s and’60s. The Thetford TPI and its
successors embrace the expected far right postures – opposing immigration and
asylum, rejecting the science of climate change, supporting book bans – and a
few more unusual ones. At their regular “truther” events in the Bell Pub,
according to [social media](https://www.rollonfriday.com/discussion/anyone-
been-thetford) reporting, they discuss the danger of chemtrails, nano-robots
in Covid vaccines, traffic crossing lights that mask millimeter-wave weapons
designed for mind control, and of course, the “great replacement theory” – the
idea that a left-wing cabal has opened national borders to colored people to
facilitate the replacement of whites. In Thetford on August 6, at the height
of the anti-immigrant attacks, a man was [heard
shouting](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/aug/06/two-men-arrested-
norfolk-police-injured-unrest-thetford-asylum-plans) “They don’t want the
white man anymore, they want to swap us.”

The far-right TPI or Council Watch group also works hand in glove with local
leaders of the Reform Party, including Scott Hussey, Norfolk County Councilor,
to oppose the housing of asylum seekers on a retired military base near
Thetford. Hussey described the anti-immigrant pogrom last week, during which
rioters threw rocks and eggs at asylum resident’s and tried to break into
their homes as "[peaceful
protest](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74g1gxvwlvo)" that merely became
"spirited." He said there were "some skirmishes" but saw no violence. Thomas
Paine, universal citizen, supporter of the commons, and advocate for free
asylum, must be turning over in his grave, wherever it is. (His bones were
stolen and [then lost](https://thomaspaine.org/faqs/where-are-paines-remains-
and-does-he-have-a-gravesite/).)

Finally, standing in front of the Paine statue in Thetford last Sunday, I
noticed a woman to my right fiddling with a cellphone mounted on a tripod. She
was well-dressed in professional black (though it was 90 degrees), and paid no
attention to me, though I was the only other person on the site. For 20
minutes or so, I walked forward and back and side to side. I also crouched,
stood on my toes, and inclined my head to better appreciate the sculpture. I
took a dozen or so photos -- some from quite close to her -- and occasionally
muttered “oh,” and “now I see.” She hardly blinked. Only experienced BBC
reporters, I thought, are so studiously oblivious to everything around them. I
later learned her name – she’s a had a good career with the Beeb- but I won’t
mention it here.

After a little while, Ms. X was joined by a colleague and together they walked
to the garden beside King’s House. I followed them, knowing something was up.
There, while her companion handled the video-camera, she interviewed Thetford
Town Councilor Matt Stirrup and the local labor MP, Terry Jermy, elected in
2024 to replace MP and Prime Minister Liz Truss. About ten minutes later, when
the BBC was finished and left, I announced my credentials and asked the two
men if they minded being detained a few minutes longer. I asked each in turn
about the recent “unrest” and their position on the asylum question.

Mr. Stirrup, a former physicians assistant, elected in 2023, told me how
saddened he was that “a lovely town like Thetford” should be in the papers and
on TV for the actions of a few bad actors. He understood why – “people of
color or with accents – not even immigrants” told him they were now scared to
go out. Kids are afraid to go to school; parents are afraid for their kids.
Then he added:

> But the idea of housing up to 1500 migrants at the former RAF Barnham base
> is a bad idea because the town hasn't the infrastructure to support them:
> not enough places in schools, not enough surgeries or dental services or
> public transportation. Plus, it’s right on the main road and would be
> dangerous for new residents. And there’s unexploded ordnance on the property
> too.

After I took a few notes, he continued:

> And there’s a marsh beside the base, so it has no room to expand if the
> population grows. Dover has a base [presumably the shuttered Connaught
> Barracks] that's much bigger and better. And besides, it’s right near the
> area where many arrive by boats. That’s a much better choice than Barnham.

MP Terry Jermy reiterated many of the same points as Stirrup. He added only
that it was time for the town to come together and heal, which was the purpose
of a
[meeting](https://www.networknorwich.co.uk/Articles/744421/Network_Norwich_and_Norfolk/Regional_News/West_Norfolk/Bishop_to_lead_Thetford_prayer_service_after.aspx)
that night at St Cuthbert's Church in the town center led by the Bishop of
Thetford.

I thanked the two men for their time and watched as they walked off together.
I’m in no position to venture an opinion whether one former military base is
better than another to house asylum seekers, but I do wonders what the
residents of Dover would say about the subject. What’s unquestionable is that
many parts of Thetford are economically deprived, and could use new people,
businesses and infrastructure. Past immigrants to Thetford have helped
revitalize a depressed downtown and could again in the future.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/thetford6-680x443.png)

Supermarkets on King Street, Thetford, August 9, 2026. Photo: The author.

But for that to happen, residents and politicians would have to heed the
advice of Paine, their native son, to “receive all who shall come, without
enquiring who or what they are.” A resettlement plan could then be devised,
(with legislation by parliament), to allow asylum seekers to work in exchange
for wages, or at least “so many meals of wholesome food, and a warm lodging,
at least as good as a barrack.” Some may then choose to save “a certain
portion” that could either be invested in the community or be the basis of a
nest egg allowing return to their native lands, if conditions permit. “Each
person,” Paine wrote, “shall stay as long or as short a time or come as often
as he choose on these conditions.”

The prospect of all that coming together seems remote – but then Paine saw the
accomplishment of revolution in two countries and profound political changes
in a third. Racism and antagonism to immigration remain strong in the U.S.,
U.K. and elsewhere today. But as Paine wrote: “Policy and interest,” may
perhaps dictate, “what reason and justice could not.”
